item.title: Gravitational Physics and Its Practical Applications

passages.title: Gravitational Physics and Its Practical Applications

paragraphs.text: The concept of gravity has evolved over time. In the seventeenth century, Isaac Newton described gravity as a universal force acting between masses, formalized in his law of universal gravitation. This theory provided a universal, mathematical framework for understanding both terrestrial and planetary motion. However, in 1915, Albert Einstein introduced general relativity, redefining gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. This shift explained phenomena Newton’s model could not, such as the bending of light near massive bodies (gravitational lensing). Einstein’s theory, which marked a revolution in physics, also predicted black holes and gravitational waves, phenomena later confirmed by observation.

paragraphs.text: Theoretical advances in gravitational physics have led to practical applications, such as in drug development. Proteins often form crystals that can be analyzed to determine their molecular structure. However, on Earth, gravity interferes with the uniform growth of crystals. In microgravity environments, such as those aboard the International Space Station (ISS), gravitational effects are minimized. Crystals grown in space tend to be larger, more uniform, and less flawed than those grown on Earth, enabling researchers to map the crystals’ atomic structure with greater accuracy. This is crucial for rational drug design, allowing scientists to develop medications that precisely target disease-related proteins.
